topics.h: When your class votes on whether the picnic should be at the zoo or at a lakeside park, you are using an idea that people have been arguing about for about 2,500 years!
p: The word democracy comes from two Greek words: 'demos' (the people) and 'kratos' (rule or power). So democracy means rule by the people.
Athens, a city-state in ancient Greece, is the best-known early democracy (around the 5th century BCE). Its citizens met in an Assembly and voted directly on laws, war and peace.
Athenian democracy was limited: only adult male citizens could take part. Women, enslaved people and foreigners living in Athens were left out.

In a direct democracy, citizens decide matters themselves. In a representative democracy, citizens elect representatives who make decisions on their behalf. Big modern countries such as India are representative democracies.
Abraham Lincoln, President of the USA, described democracy in 1863 as 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'.

ex.q: Think it through: Citizens of Athens could gather in one place and vote on every law. Why can't all voters of India do the same today?
st: Athens was a single city, and the number of citizens who could take part was fairly small.
India is a huge country with crores of voters spread over villages, towns and cities.
It is impossible for all of them to meet together and debate every law, every day.
So Indians elect representatives (MPs, MLAs, councillors, panchayat members) who discuss and decide for them and answer to them at the next election.
ex.a: Because of India's huge size and population, direct democracy for every decision is not practical, so India uses representative democracy.

topics.rl: A school student council, a housing society committee and a gram sabha meeting in a village are all small examples of people taking part in decisions, either directly or through people they choose.

rv.summary: Democracy means rule by the people, from the Greek 'demos' (people) and 'kratos' (rule). Ancient Athens practised a limited direct democracy; big modern countries like India are representative democracies.

topics.h: Long before ballot boxes, a village in Tamil Nadu chose its leaders by pulling palm-leaf slips out of a pot. India's democratic story is very old!
p: The Rigveda mentions assemblies called the sabha and the samiti, where members of the community met to discuss common matters.

Around the 6th century BCE, some states in north India were ganas or sanghas, governed by an assembly of many people instead of a single king. The Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy, with its capital at Vaishali in present-day Bihar, is a well-known example.
The Buddhist sangha took decisions in meetings of monks, following rules for discussion and voting.

Inscriptions at Uttaramerur in Tamil Nadu, from the Chola period (10th century CE), describe how members of the village assembly were chosen: names were written on palm leaves, put in a pot and drawn out. This was called kudavolai.

Modern India's Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950 and gave universal adult franchise: every adult citizen got the right to vote, whatever their religion, caste, gender, wealth or education.

ex.q: Think it through: Why are the Uttaramerur inscriptions important for understanding democracy in India?
st: They are written records carved in stone, so they give solid evidence and not just stories.
They describe rules for choosing members of a village assembly and the qualifications needed.
This shows that ideas such as choosing members by a fixed, written procedure existed in India over a thousand years ago.
Such traditions are part of the background to India's modern democracy.
ex.a: They are clear evidence that Indian villages had rule-based ways of choosing assembly members over 1,000 years ago.

topics.rl: Gram sabhas and panchayats in Indian villages today continue the old tradition of local communities discussing and deciding their own matters.

rv.summary: India has old democratic roots: Rigvedic sabha and samiti, ganas like the Vajji confederacy at Vaishali, the Buddhist sangha, and Chola-era kudavolai elections at Uttaramerur. The Constitution (26 January 1950) gave universal adult franchise.

topics.h: If one person decided everything in your school, from the timetable to the canteen menu, and nobody could complain, would you be happy? Democracy is about having a say.
p: In a democracy, rulers are chosen by the people in free and fair elections held regularly, and voters have a real choice. Every adult has one vote and each vote has equal value.
Rule of law: the law applies equally to everyone, including those in power. Fundamental rights of citizens are protected by the Constitution and the courts.
Separation of powers divides work among the legislature (makes laws), the executive (carries them out) and the judiciary (interprets laws and settles disputes), so that no one holds all power.
Accountability and transparency: the government must answer to the people and work openly. The Right to Information Act, 2005 lets citizens ask for government information.

Democracy is valued because it makes governments answerable, allows peaceful change, respects dignity and equality, and lets mistakes be corrected. Its challenges include slow decisions, misuse of money and misinformation, and protecting the rights of weaker groups.
A free media and grassroots democracy (panchayats and municipalities, given constitutional status by the 73rd and 74th Amendments in 1992) keep citizens informed and involved.

ex.q: Think it through: Country X holds an election every five years, but the ruling party jails all opposition candidates before voting day. Is Country X a democracy?
st: Holding an election is necessary for democracy, but it is not enough.
The election must be free and fair, and people must have a real choice between candidates.
If opposition candidates are jailed, voters cannot really choose and the rulers cannot be voted out.
So the rulers are not truly accountable to the people.
ex.a: No. Without a free and fair election and real choice, Country X is not a democracy even though it holds elections.

topics.rl: When a news report exposes a broken road, citizens file an RTI application, or a gram sabha questions how village funds were spent, democracy is working at the everyday level.

rv.summary: A democracy has free and fair elections with equal votes, rule of law, protected rights, separation of powers, accountability and transparency. It is valued because governments answer to people and can be changed peacefully, though decisions can be slow.

topics.h: India's general election is one of the biggest events organised anywhere on Earth: polling teams carry machines by road, boat and on foot so that even remote voters can vote!
p: India is divided into areas called constituencies. The Lok Sabha has 543 constituencies, and each elects one Member of Parliament (MP). Each state is also divided into assembly constituencies that elect MLAs. Elections are normally held every 5 years.
Every citizen aged 18 or above whose name is on the electoral roll (voter list) can vote. Voting is secret, and an indelible ink mark on the finger helps prevent anyone voting twice.

The Election Commission of India (ECI), set up on 25 January 1950 under Article 324 of the Constitution, is an independent body that conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President.

Main steps: dates are announced and the Model Code of Conduct begins, candidates file nominations, nominations are checked, campaigning takes place, people vote on polling day, and votes are counted and results declared.
Votes are cast on Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs). A VVPAT machine prints a slip showing the chosen symbol so the voter can check it. NOTA ('None of the Above') lets a voter reject all candidates.
Some constituencies are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes: only candidates from these groups can contest there, but all voters of the constituency vote.

ex.q: Think it through: Why is voting in India kept secret?
st: If others could see how someone voted, powerful people could threaten or bribe voters.
Secrecy lets every voter choose freely, without fear of their boss, neighbours or even family.
This protects the freedom and fairness of the election.
ex.a: Secret voting protects voters from pressure and fear, so that every vote is a free choice.

topics.rl: National Voters' Day is celebrated on 25 January, the day the Election Commission was set up. Ask an adult at home to show you the voter ID card (EPIC) and the ink mark after voting.

rv.summary: India is divided into constituencies; the Lok Sabha has 543, each electing one MP, normally every 5 years. Citizens aged 18+ on the electoral roll vote secretly on EVMs with VVPAT. The independent Election Commission of India, set up on 25 January 1950, conducts elections.

topics.h: In a race, the runner who crosses the line first wins, even if just by a step. India's Lok Sabha elections work in a similar way!
p: First-Past-The-Post (FPTP): the country is divided into constituencies, each electing one representative. The candidate with the most votes wins, even with less than half of all votes.
Under FPTP, a party's share of seats can be very different from its share of votes, because only the winner in each constituency gets the seat.

Proportional Representation (PR): a party gets seats in proportion to its share of votes. In list PR, used in countries such as Israel and the Netherlands, votes are counted for parties, and each party's seats are filled from its list of candidates.

India uses FPTP for Lok Sabha and state Vidhan Sabha elections. It uses PR by single transferable vote (voters rank candidates by preference) to elect Rajya Sabha members (by MLAs), the President and the Vice-President.
India chose FPTP for direct elections because it is simple for voters, gives every area its own representative, and usually produces clear results and stable governments.

ex.q: Think it through: In a constituency, Asha gets 42,000 votes, Bilal 38,000 and Charan 20,000 (total 1,00,000). Who wins under FPTP, and did the winner get a majority?
st: Under FPTP, the candidate with the highest number of votes wins.
Asha has the most votes (42,000), so Asha wins the seat.
42% is less than half, so 58% of voters chose someone else, yet Asha still wins.
ex.a: Asha wins with 42% of the votes, which is the most votes but not a majority.

topics.rl: When results are shown on TV, the Lok Sabha seat count of a party is often very different from its percentage of votes. That is FPTP at work.

rv.summary: Under First-Past-The-Post, each constituency elects one member and the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority. Under proportional representation, parties get seats in proportion to their votes. India uses FPTP for Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections.

topics.h: For about 21 months, from 1975 to 1977, many rights that Indians took for granted were suspended. Then voters had their say at the ballot box. This chapter of our history shows why democratic safeguards matter.
p: The Constitution allows a national emergency under Article 352 when the country faces a grave threat. During an emergency, the central government gets extra powers and some fundamental rights can be suspended.

Background: on 12 June 1975, the Allahabad High Court declared Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's 1971 election from Rae Bareli void. At the same time, a large opposition movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan was demanding her resignation.

On 25 June 1975, President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed a national emergency on the grounds of 'internal disturbance', on the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The government said this was needed to maintain order and stability.

During the Emergency, many fundamental rights were suspended, newspapers were censored, many opposition leaders and others were detained without trial, and elections were postponed. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made many changes to the Constitution.

Lok Sabha elections were held in March 1977. The ruling Congress lost, and the Emergency was withdrawn on 21 March 1977. The Janata Party formed the government, and Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress Prime Minister.

The 44th Amendment (1978) added safeguards: 'internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion', the President can declare an emergency only on the written advice of the Cabinet, and the rights in Articles 20 and 21 (including life and personal liberty) cannot be suspended.

ex.q: Think it through: What lessons did India's democracy learn from the Emergency?
st: It showed that the emergency powers in the Constitution could be used to suspend rights for a long time.
It showed how important a free press, independent courts and the right to protest are in a democracy.
In 1977, voters used their vote to change the government peacefully.
Parliament then passed the 44th Amendment so that emergency powers would be harder to misuse.
ex.a: Rights need strong safeguards, citizens and institutions must stay alert, and elections let people change governments peacefully.

topics.rl: Whenever people discuss press freedom, the independence of courts or limits on government power, the experience of 1975–77 is often remembered.

rv.summary: On 25 June 1975, President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed a national emergency under Article 352 on PM Indira Gandhi's advice. Rights were suspended, the press censored and opposition leaders detained. In 1977 voters defeated Congress; the 44th Amendment added safeguards.

topics.t: What governance means and who governs
topics.h: Clean water from the tap, a streetlight that works, a school bus that runs on time: each one is a small sign of governance quietly doing its job!
p: Government means the institutions that hold the authority to make and enforce decisions for the country: the legislature makes laws, the executive puts them into action, and the judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes. India has governments at the Union, state and local levels.

Governance means the whole process of making decisions, carrying them out and checking whether they worked, for the welfare of the public. Simply put, government is the institution; governance is how the work actually gets done.

Many people take part in governance: elected representatives, ministries and departments, civil servants, courts, panchayats and municipalities, and also citizens, the media, civil society groups, researchers and businesses.

Principles of good governance include participation, transparency (decisions and information are open), accountability (those in authority answer for their actions), the rule of law (the same laws apply equally to all), responsiveness, inclusiveness and effectiveness.

Indian traditions have long discussed just rule. Rajadharma is the duty of a ruler to protect the people and work for their welfare, and Mahatma Gandhi used 'Ram Rajya' to describe an ideal of fair rule where even the weakest person gets justice. India's national motto 'Satyameva Jayate' ('Truth alone triumphs') comes from the Mundaka Upanishad. The Sengol, a ceremonial sceptre that stands for just rule in the Tamil tradition, was installed in the new Parliament building in 2023.

ex.q: Think it through: After a night of very heavy rain, roads in a town are flooded. Is this a job for just one office?
st: The municipal body must clear the drains and pump out water.
Traffic police must divert vehicles, and the electricity department must make fallen wires safe.
The health department must prevent water-borne diseases, and disaster response teams may need to rescue people.
All of them must share information and work together, and residents must be told what to do.
ex.a: No. Handling the flood needs many departments to coordinate and communicate. That coordinated process of deciding, acting and checking is governance.

topics.rl: In Delhi, the Delhi Jal Board is a government body; how it plans the water supply, tests water quality and fixes complaints is governance. The same is true of your town's municipal body collecting waste every morning.

rv.summary: Government is the institution (legislature, executive, judiciary); governance is the process of deciding, acting and checking for public welfare. Good governance means participation, transparency, accountability, rule of law, responsiveness, inclusiveness and effectiveness.

topics.h: Why does your school bus stop exactly where it does, and why is there a zebra crossing outside your school? Someone had to notice a problem, think of options and decide!
p: A public policy is a planned course of action taken by the government to solve a public problem or meet a public need. It is 'public' because it uses public resources and affects society. A company's work-from-home rule is a policy, but not a public policy.

A policy sets the broad goals and direction. Programmes and schemes are specific plans that put a policy into action. For example, Khelo Bharat Niti 2025 is India's national sports policy, and it involves several ministries, such as Youth Affairs and Sports, and Education.

Policies usually move through a cycle: identify the problem or need, set priorities, consult stakeholders and draft options (formulation), get formal approval (adoption), put it into action (implementation), monitor and evaluate, and use feedback to revise the policy.

Stakeholders are people and groups affected by or involved in a policy, such as citizens, elected representatives, departments, local bodies, experts, civil society, the media and businesses. Consulting them makes a policy more practical and fair.

Money, staff and time are limited, so governments must set priorities and check feasibility: Is it affordable? Is it technically possible? Who will carry it out? Evidence and data help decide what comes first.

ex.q: Think it through: Every morning there is a traffic jam at your school gate. How could a policy be made to fix it?
st: Identify the problem: collect facts, such as how many vehicles arrive between 7:30 and 8:00.
Consult stakeholders: parents, students, teachers, bus drivers, traffic police and nearby shopkeepers.
Draft options: a separate drop-off zone, different arrival times for different classes, more school buses, a walking group for nearby students.
Check feasibility (cost, space, safety), choose the best option, and get the principal and school committee to approve it.
Try it out, check whether the jam reduces, and change the plan if needed.
ex.a: Follow the policy cycle: identify, consult, draft options, choose and adopt, implement, then check and improve.

topics.rl: The Swachh Bharat Mission, launched on 2 October 2014, aimed to make India clean and free from open defecation. It needed the Union government, states, municipalities, panchayats and ordinary citizens to work together.

topics.t: Putting policies into action and checking results
topics.h: A village planted 1,000 saplings and celebrated. A year later, most had dried up. Was the policy a success? It depends on what you count!
p: Implementation means putting an approved policy into action. It is mainly done by the executive: ministries, departments, civil servants, district administrations and local bodies such as panchayats and municipalities. It needs money in the budget, trained people, clear rules and good coordination.
Many policies need several agencies to work together. For road safety near a school, the school, traffic police, road authorities and parents all have a part to play.
Monitoring means tracking progress while a policy is being carried out. Evaluation means judging, after some time, whether the policy achieved its goals and what its impact was.

An output is what was done (saplings planted, toilets built). An outcome is the real change (saplings surviving, toilets being used, fewer illnesses). Good evaluation checks outcomes and how different groups, such as girls, rural families or persons with disabilities, benefited.

Feedback and complaints show where a policy is falling short, so it can be revised. In a social audit, the community checks the records of a scheme in a public meeting. E-governance uses digital technology to deliver services, such as DigiLocker for documents, IRCTC for train tickets and the Parivahan portal for vehicle services, but people without internet access or digital skills still need offline help.

ex.q: Think it through: A ward planted 1,000 saplings. After one year, only 350 were alive. What went wrong, and how can it be fixed?
st: The output looked good: 1,000 saplings planted.
The outcome was weak: 1,000 - 350 = 650 saplings died.
Likely causes: no plan for watering, no tree guards, and no one responsible for checking survival.
Fix: give one agency clear responsibility, budget for watering and guards, involve residents, and monitor survival every few months.
ex.a: Implementation and monitoring were weak. Counting plantings is not enough; survival (the outcome) must be planned for and checked.

topics.rl: Many services that once needed long queues can now be done online: you can book train tickets on IRCTC, and families can keep marksheets and other certificates in DigiLocker. Common Service Centres help people who cannot do this on their own.

rv.summary: Implementation puts an approved policy into action, mainly through the executive and local bodies, often with several agencies. Monitoring tracks progress; evaluation judges outcomes later. Feedback, social audits and e-governance help, but offline help is still needed.

topics.h: You don't need to be a minister to improve governance. Reporting one broken streetlight can make a whole lane safer!
p: Voting is important, but citizens' role does not end on election day. Between elections, people can give feedback, take part in public consultations, raise complaints and suggest ideas.

In villages, the Gram Sabha includes every adult whose name is on the voter list of the village or panchayat area. It discusses village plans and reviews the work done. The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to panchayats and municipalities.

The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 lets any citizen ask a public authority for information. A reply is normally due within 30 days, or within 48 hours if a person's life or liberty is involved. This supports transparency and accountability.
Citizens can lodge complaints online through CPGRAMS (the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System), use helplines, and share ideas on programmes through the MyGov platform.

Everyday duties also matter: following rules, paying taxes, saving water and electricity, safeguarding public property (a Fundamental Duty) and checking information before forwarding it. Students can join student councils, cleanliness drives and road-safety campaigns.

ex.q: Think it through: The streetlight on your lane has not worked for two weeks. What can your family do?
st: Note the exact location and the pole number, if there is one.
Report it to the municipal helpline, app or website, or tell the ward councillor.
Keep the complaint number and follow up if nothing happens.
If there is still no action, an RTI application can ask for the status of the complaint.
ex.a: Report it through the proper channel, keep a record, and follow up. Active citizens help governance work better.

topics.rl: National Good Governance Day is observed on 25 December, the birth anniversary of former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee. In the Swachh Survekshan cleanliness survey, citizens' feedback is part of how cities are ranked; Indore and Surat were jointly ranked the cleanest cities in Swachh Survekshan 2023.

rv.summary: Citizens' role in governance goes beyond voting: they take part in Gram Sabhas, use RTI, file complaints on CPGRAMS, share ideas on MyGov, and do everyday duties like paying taxes, saving resources, safeguarding public property and checking information before sharing.

qa.q: The Greek word 'demos', from which 'democracy' comes, means:
qa.a: The people
qa.e: 'Demos' means the people and 'kratos' means rule or power. Together they give 'rule by the people'.

qa.q: Which ancient city-state is best known as an early democracy where citizens voted directly on laws?
qa.a: Athens
qa.e: In Athens, around the 5th century BCE, citizens met in an Assembly and voted directly on important matters.

qa.q: Who could take part in the Assembly of ancient Athens?
qa.a: Adult male citizens
qa.e: Only adult male citizens could vote in Athens. Women, enslaved people and foreign residents were excluded, so it was a limited democracy.

qa.q: In which form of democracy do citizens elect people to make laws on their behalf?
qa.a: Representative democracy
qa.e: In a representative democracy, voters choose representatives such as MPs and MLAs who make laws for them.

qa.q: Why do large countries like India use representative democracy rather than direct democracy?
qa.a: Crores of citizens cannot all meet and decide every matter together
qa.e: With crores of voters spread across a vast country, it is not practical for everyone to debate and vote on every law, so people elect representatives.

qa.q: Who described democracy as 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'?
qa.a: Abraham Lincoln
qa.e: US President Abraham Lincoln used these words in his Gettysburg Address in 1863.

qa.q: All 40 families of a housing society meet and vote together on whether to build a children's park. This is an example of:
qa.a: Direct democracy
qa.e: Every member votes on the decision personally, without choosing representatives, so it is direct democracy.

qa.q: Roughly how long ago did democracy flourish in ancient Athens?
qa.a: About 2,500 years ago
qa.e: Athenian democracy flourished around the 5th century BCE, which is roughly 2,500 years ago.

qa.q: Which ancient text mentions the assemblies called sabha and samiti?
qa.a: The Rigveda
qa.e: The sabha and samiti are Vedic assemblies mentioned in the Rigveda.

qa.q: What was special about a gana or sangha in ancient India?
qa.a: It was governed by an assembly of many people, not by one hereditary king
qa.e: In ganas or sanghas, decisions were taken by an assembly of members rather than a single king.

qa.q: Vaishali, capital of the Vajji confederacy, is in which present-day state?
qa.a: Bihar
qa.e: Vaishali is in present-day Bihar, in the middle Ganga plains where several ganas existed.

qa.q: Uttaramerur, famous for inscriptions about village assembly elections, is in:
qa.a: Tamil Nadu
qa.e: Uttaramerur is in Tamil Nadu. Its Chola-period inscriptions describe how village assembly members were chosen.

qa.q: How did the kudavolai system at Uttaramerur work?
qa.a: Names written on palm leaves were put in a pot and drawn out
qa.e: Names of eligible people were written on palm leaves, placed in a pot (kudam) and drawn out, so the choice followed a fixed procedure.

qa.q: Universal adult franchise in India means:
qa.a: Every adult citizen has the right to vote, without discrimination
qa.e: From 1950, every adult citizen got the vote, irrespective of religion, caste, gender, wealth or education.

qa.q: What is the minimum age to vote in India today?
qa.a: 18 years
qa.e: The 61st Constitutional Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years.

qa.q: When were the first general elections of independent India held?
qa.e: The first general elections were held between October 1951 and February 1952, after the Constitution came into force in 1950.

qa.q: The principle 'one person, one vote, one value' means:
qa.a: Every adult's vote counts equally
qa.e: Every adult citizen has one vote, and every vote carries the same weight.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of accountability in a democracy?
qa.a: Ministers answering questions asked by members in Parliament
qa.e: Accountability means those in power must explain and answer for their actions, for example during Question Hour in Parliament.

qa.q: A minister's car jumps a red light and the minister is fined just like any other driver. This shows:
qa.a: Rule of law
qa.e: Rule of law means the same law applies to everyone, including people in power.

qa.q: Which organ of government interprets laws and settles disputes?
qa.a: The judiciary
qa.e: The judiciary (the courts) interprets laws and settles disputes. The legislature makes laws and the executive carries them out.

qa.q: Which is the strongest reason why democracy is considered better than other forms of government?
qa.a: The government is answerable to the people and can be changed peacefully
qa.e: Democracy does not guarantee perfect leaders, but it makes governments answerable and lets people change them through elections.

qa.q: Which is a common criticism of democracy?
qa.a: Decisions can take longer because of debate and consultation
qa.e: Because many people are consulted and debate takes time, decisions in a democracy can be slow.

qa.q: How does a free media help democracy?
qa.a: It informs citizens and can expose wrongdoing by those in power
qa.e: A free press keeps people informed and holds the powerful to account by reporting on their actions.

qa.q: In which year was the Right to Information Act passed, letting citizens ask for government information?
qa.e: The Right to Information Act was passed in 2005 to promote transparency in government.

qa.q: Which body conducts elections to the Lok Sabha?
qa.a: The Election Commission of India
qa.e: The Election Commission of India conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. State Election Commissions conduct panchayat and municipal elections.

qa.q: What does a VVPAT machine do?
qa.a: Prints a slip showing the symbol the voter chose, so the voter can check it
qa.e: VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) shows a printed slip of the chosen symbol for a few seconds so the voter can verify the vote.

qa.q: What is the Model Code of Conduct?
qa.a: Guidelines that parties, candidates and governments must follow during elections
qa.e: It is a set of guidelines from the Election Commission. For example, the government should not announce new schemes to win votes once elections are announced.

qa.q: What does pressing NOTA on an EVM mean?
qa.a: The voter rejects all the candidates
qa.e: NOTA stands for 'None of the Above'. It lets a voter record that they do not support any candidate. It was added in 2013 after a Supreme Court judgment.

qa.q: In a constituency reserved for Scheduled Castes, who can vote?
qa.a: All registered voters of that constituency
qa.e: Reservation decides who can contest, not who can vote. Only Scheduled Caste candidates can stand, but every registered voter there votes.

qa.q: What is an electoral roll?
qa.a: The list of people eligible to vote in a constituency
qa.e: The electoral roll, or voter list, contains the names of all eligible voters. It is updated regularly.

qa.q: Why is indelible ink put on a voter's finger?
qa.a: To stop the same person from voting twice
qa.e: The ink mark cannot be removed easily for many days, so polling staff can see that the person has already voted.

qa.q: The Election Commission of India was set up on 25 January of which year?
qa.e: It was set up on 25 January 1950, a day before the Constitution came into force. National Voters' Day is celebrated on this date.

qa.q: In a constituency, Asha gets 42,000 votes, Bilal 38,000 and Charan 20,000. Who wins under FPTP?
qa.a: Asha
qa.e: Under FPTP the candidate with the most votes wins. A majority (more than half) is not needed.

qa.q: In the same contest (42,000 + 38,000 + 20,000 votes), what percentage of the votes did the winner get?
qa.e: 42,000 out of 1,00,000 votes is 42%. So the winner won with less than half of the votes.

qa.q: A legislature has 200 seats and uses pure proportional representation. A party wins 25% of the votes. About how many seats should it get?
qa.e: Under PR, seats follow vote share: 25% of 200 = 50 seats.

qa.q: Which elections in India are held using the First-Past-The-Post system?
qa.a: Lok Sabha elections
qa.e: Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections use FPTP. The President, Vice-President and Rajya Sabha members are elected by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.

qa.q: How is the President of India elected?
qa.a: By an electoral college through proportional representation by single transferable vote
qa.e: Elected MPs and elected MLAs form the electoral college, and they vote using the single transferable vote, a form of PR.

qa.q: What is a major drawback of the FPTP system?
qa.a: A party's share of seats can be much larger or smaller than its share of votes
qa.e: In FPTP only the winner in each constituency gets the seat, so votes for losing candidates do not turn into seats.

qa.q: Why did India choose FPTP for Lok Sabha elections?
qa.a: It is simple for voters and gives each area its own representative
qa.e: FPTP is easy to understand, links each constituency with one accountable representative, and tends to give clear results.

qa.q: Which country uses proportional representation with the whole country treated as one constituency?
qa.a: Israel
qa.e: In Israel, seats in its parliament are shared out among parties according to their national vote share. India, the UK and Canada use FPTP for their national parliament elections.

qa.q: On which date was the national emergency proclaimed in 1975?
qa.a: 25 June 1975
qa.e: The Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court had given its verdict on the Rae Bareli election.

qa.q: Who was the President of India who proclaimed the Emergency in 1975?
qa.a: Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
qa.e: President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed the Emergency on the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

qa.q: Under which Article number of the Constitution can a national emergency be proclaimed?
qa.e: Article 352 deals with a national emergency. Article 356 is about President's Rule in a state and Article 360 about financial emergency.

qa.q: Which of these happened during the Emergency of 1975–77?
qa.a: Newspapers were censored and many opposition leaders were detained
qa.e: Press censorship and detention of opposition leaders without trial were major features of the Emergency.

qa.q: Who led the large opposition movement in 1974–75 that demanded the Prime Minister's resignation?
qa.a: Jayaprakash Narayan
qa.e: Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) led the movement. Ambedkar, Patel and Rajendra Prasad had passed away before the 1970s.

qa.q: What was the result of the Lok Sabha elections of March 1977?
qa.a: The Janata Party formed the government and Morarji Desai became Prime Minister
qa.e: Voters defeated the ruling Congress. The Janata Party formed the first non-Congress government at the Centre, led by Morarji Desai.

qa.q: What change did the 44th Amendment (1978) make to emergency provisions?
qa.a: 'Internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion' as a ground
qa.e: The 44th Amendment narrowed the grounds to war, external aggression or armed rebellion, and added other safeguards.

qa.q: About how long did the Emergency of 1975–77 last?
qa.a: About 21 months
qa.e: It lasted from 25 June 1975 to March 1977, which is about 21 months.

qa.q: Which statement best describes governance?
qa.a: The process of making, carrying out and checking decisions for public welfare
qa.e: Governance is the whole process of deciding, acting and monitoring for the public good. It is ongoing, not a single building, event or party.

qa.q: Which organ of government mainly puts laws and policies into action?
qa.a: The executive
qa.e: The executive (ministers, ministries, departments and civil servants) implements laws and policies. The legislature makes laws and the judiciary interprets them.

qa.q: A city department puts its full budget and spending details on its website for anyone to read. Which principle of good governance does this show most clearly?
qa.a: Transparency
qa.e: Making information about decisions and spending open to the public is transparency.

qa.q: In the state assembly, members question a minister about why a scheme failed, and the minister must explain. Which principle is at work?
qa.a: Accountability
qa.e: Accountability means those in authority must answer for their decisions and actions. Questions in the legislature are one way of holding the executive accountable.

qa.q: What does 'Rajadharma' mean?
qa.a: The duty of a ruler to protect the people and work for their welfare
qa.e: Rajadharma is the idea that a ruler's power comes with duties: protecting the people and working for their well-being.

qa.q: India's national motto 'Satyameva Jayate' is taken from which text?
qa.a: The Mundaka Upanishad
qa.e: 'Satyameva Jayate', meaning 'Truth alone triumphs', comes from the Mundaka Upanishad. It is written below the Lion Capital in the State Emblem of India.

qa.q: Who takes part in governance?
qa.a: Government institutions along with citizens, the media, civil society and others
qa.e: Governance involves government institutions at every level, and also citizens, the media, civil society groups, researchers and businesses.

qa.q: A town builds ramps, Braille signs and accessible toilets at its bus stand so that persons with disabilities can use it easily. Which principle does this show?
qa.a: Inclusiveness
qa.e: Inclusiveness means public services are designed so that no group, including persons with disabilities, is left out.

qa.q: What is a public policy?
qa.a: A planned course of action by the government to solve a public problem or meet a public need
qa.e: A public policy is made by the government, uses public resources and affects society as a whole.

qa.q: Which of these is a public policy?
qa.a: A national policy on vaccinating children
qa.e: A national vaccination policy is made by the government for the whole society. The others are rules of private groups or families.

qa.q: Which stage usually comes FIRST when a public policy is made?
qa.a: Identifying the problem or need
qa.e: A policy begins by identifying a problem or need. Only then can options be drafted, adopted and implemented.

qa.q: What happens during the formulation stage of a policy?
qa.a: Stakeholders are consulted, options are drafted and their cost and feasibility are checked
qa.e: Formulation means preparing the policy: consulting, drafting options and checking whether they are affordable and practical.

qa.q: Why should a government consult stakeholders before finalising a policy?
qa.a: Because people who are affected know the problem first-hand, which makes the policy more practical and fair
qa.e: People affected by a problem often understand it best. Their views help avoid mistakes and make the policy work in real life.

qa.q: How is a policy different from a programme or scheme?
qa.a: A policy sets broad goals and direction; a programme is a specific plan to achieve them
qa.e: The policy gives the big picture and goals. Programmes and schemes are the detailed plans that turn those goals into action.

qa.q: Why do governments have to set priorities among public needs?
qa.a: Because money, staff and time are limited, so the most urgent needs must be met first
qa.e: Resources are limited, so governments use evidence to decide which needs are most urgent, such as safe drinking water.

qa.q: What does 'adoption' of a policy mean?
qa.a: The policy is formally approved by the proper authority, such as the Cabinet, a legislature or a municipal council
qa.e: Adoption is the formal approval of a policy by the authority that has the power to decide, after which it can be implemented.

qa.q: Who mainly implements public policies?
qa.a: Ministries, departments, civil servants and local bodies
qa.e: Implementation is the work of the executive: ministries, departments, civil servants, district offices, panchayats and municipalities.

qa.q: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation?
qa.a: Monitoring tracks progress while a policy runs; evaluation judges its results and impact later
qa.e: Monitoring is ongoing tracking during implementation. Evaluation looks back to judge whether goals were achieved.

qa.q: A ward installed 40 public water taps. A survey found that 30 of them were working. How many taps were NOT working?
qa.e: Taps not working = 40 - 30 = 10. Finding such gaps is exactly what monitoring is for.

qa.q: Which of these is an OUTCOME rather than an output of a clean-water policy?
qa.a: Fewer children falling ill with diarrhoea
qa.e: An outcome is a real change in people's lives, such as better health. Pipelines, money and meetings are inputs or outputs.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of e-governance?
qa.a: Getting a vehicle-related service on the Parivahan portal
qa.e: E-governance is the use of digital technology to deliver government services. The Parivahan portal offers vehicle-related services online.

qa.q: A certificate service is made online-only. What problem might this create?
qa.a: People without internet access or digital skills may be left out, so offline help is also needed
qa.e: Not everyone has a smartphone, internet or digital skills. Inclusive governance keeps help centres or offline options for them.

qa.q: What happens in a social audit?
qa.a: Local people check the records of a government scheme in a public meeting
qa.e: In a social audit, the community examines records of a scheme, such as work done and money spent, to check that they match reality.

qa.q: A tree-planting drive counted saplings planted but never checked how many survived. What was the main weakness?
qa.a: Monitoring looked only at outputs, and no one was responsible for watering and protecting the saplings
qa.e: Counting plantings measures only the output. Without care after planting and checks on survival, the real goal, a greener area, is not met.

qa.q: Which of these is a way for citizens to take part in governance BETWEEN elections?
qa.a: Attending a Gram Sabha meeting to discuss village plans
qa.e: Gram Sabha meetings let villagers discuss plans and review work. Participation continues between elections.

qa.q: Who are the members of a Gram Sabha?
qa.a: All adults whose names are on the voter list of the village or panchayat area
qa.e: The Gram Sabha is made up of every adult registered as a voter in the village or panchayat area, so it is the village's own assembly.

qa.q: What does the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 allow?
qa.a: Any citizen can ask public authorities for information
qa.e: Under the RTI Act, any citizen can seek information from public authorities, which makes government more transparent and accountable.

qa.q: Under the RTI Act, within how much time should a normal request usually be answered?
qa.a: 30 days
qa.e: A reply is normally due within 30 days. If a person's life or liberty is involved, it must be given within 48 hours.

qa.q: National Good Governance Day is observed every year on:
qa.a: 25 December
qa.e: Good Governance Day is observed on 25 December, the birth anniversary of former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee.

qa.q: Which is the most helpful thing a student can do to support good governance?
qa.a: Check whether information is true before sharing it
qa.e: Checking information before forwarding stops rumours, which helps people and authorities make good decisions.

qa.q: Which of these is one of the Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens?
qa.a: To safeguard public property
qa.e: Safeguarding public property and avoiding violence is a Fundamental Duty listed in Article 51A of the Constitution.

qa.q: Why is feedback from citizens useful to the government?
qa.a: Citizens use services every day and notice problems that officials may miss
qa.e: People who use a service daily see its gaps first. Their feedback helps departments fix problems and improve policies.
